message.content: {"name":"drop_out","parameters":{"public_message":"Out. Dead red, not worth my cash.","private_thought":"Illinois splits three ways (Kentucky p1, Indiana p2 mortgaged). Winning at $141+ drops me to $518 or less, wiping the buffer over PP 2h ($500). p2 still has $309 after $140 and can build PP to 3h ($200) before I roll; BW 3h ($1400) and PP 3h ($1100) already kill me. Do not win a dead deed. Keep cash for Virginia ($160) pink set and a PP 2h hit. Do not sell St. Charles, States, or Baltic. Do not pay p2."}}
message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to bid on Illinois Avenue in the auction.

I passed on the $240 bid because the red group is incomplete. Kentucky and Indiana are already owned by other players, so I would not have a full set. The current high bid is $140, but I still need to evaluate whether to raise it.

No player can complete a red monopoly without trading with both p1 and p2. I have enough cash to cover the $500 rent on Park Place, but Boardwalk would still be lethal.

I would rather spend cash on Virginia or Med to complete my pink and brown monopolies. Illinois would not help me build a set, and it would reduce my buffer against dark blue rent. The main threat is p2 with their dark blue monopoly, not the auction.

Raising the bid would drain p2's cash. They still have enough to build another house on Park Place even after paying $140 for Illinois.

I should not bid enough to actually win the property. I need to keep my cash above the $500 rent on Park Place with a safety buffer. p4 already owns the full light blue set and could build houses there.

p4 owns Atlantic and Ventnor in the yellow group, but still needs Marvin Gardens to complete it. Pacific is a green property, not yellow. p1 holds two of the three orange spaces.

Winning Illinois for about $150 would leave me with only $18 of cash above the $500 rent on Park Place. That is too risky. Even a modest bid of $141 leaves just $18 buffer. I should not raise the price enough to actually win.

The best move is to drop out. I considered bidding once to push p2 higher, but the other players are all quick to bid, so that would likely backfire and leave me stuck with the property.

I checked the exact rent schedule. Park Place with three houses costs $1100, which would bankrupt me if p2 builds there. Boardwalk at three houses costs $1400, also lethal. This confirms that p2 must be prevented from building on either property.

p2 already passed their turn on turn 34. After the auction I end my turn, then p4 and p1 go. p2 will roll again before I do. If they build a house on Park Place after paying for Illinois, the rent jumps to $1100 and kills me.

Bidding to about $250 would leave p2 with less than $200 after paying for Illinois. That is below the $200 cost of a house, so they could not build on Park Place before I roll again. This would block their next house and prevent the rent jump to $1100.

Winning at $250 would leave me with only $409, which is still below the $500 rent on Park Place. p2 would still have enough cash to build a third house there and kill me anyway.

I should not bid high enough to actually win. I need to push the price up so p2 or another player pays heavily, but stay safely below the $100–140 range.

p1 has $643 and owns Kentucky in the red group. He may want Illinois as a trade chip or to block p2 from completing a red monopoly.

p4 has $849 and no reds, so their low bid may be speculative. p2 owns mortgaged Indiana, making Illinois a trade chip rather than a priority. A bid of $160 would leave me with only one dollar above the $500 rent on Park Place, which is catastrophic if I land there. Even winning at $150 would leave just nine dollars of buffer. The risk is too high.

I should not sell St. Charles, States, or Baltic to p2. Dropping out is the safest play. If I bid and win, I would own a useless property. The downside is that p2 keeps building money.

A bid of $200 would likely backfire. The other players are bidding in small increments, so they probably would not chase that high. I would end up winning the property for $200 and left with only $459, which cannot cover the $500 rent on Park Place. Dropping out is the only safe choice.
